result.summary: Zero deviations are a reporting artifact, not quality improvement. The February 2026 supervisor bonus penalty preceded the collapse of NCRs, while independent QC rejections (0.8% to 1.3%) and complaints (11 to 31 ppm) rose. Line 3's output edge is not transferable practice: badge data shows borrowed Line 1 and 4 technicians, with flat output per technician-hour. The hotline report describes undocumented rework on Line 3, and 71% of traceable luer-leak complaints come from Line 3 lots. The tubing switch fits poorly, since it came after the complaint rise began and affects all lines. Do not roll out Line 3 or unmask the reporter. Remove the penalty, offer amnesty, and run an independent investigation including shipped-lot risk. Whether the Plant Manager directs the lending is not established.

Ticket records contradict deprioritisation of Arts. SlotBook tickets (42% of Arts volume, none from other faculties) were all routed to P4 with a 21-day median. They account for about 70% of the resolution gap. Arts non-SlotBook tickets match non-Arts tickets within 0.3 days by category and priority. The remaining gap comes from Tuesday/Thursday-only Lindqvist technician coverage, which Education also experiences. Duplicate rates are similar, so the trivial-ticket claim is unsupported. ACK-P4 tells requesters nothing about priority or timeframe. Whether Arts leadership was told of RR-17 is unestablished: one uncorroborated meeting, no records, and the former manager declined to be interviewed. The SSO link to the SlotBook rise is confounded by term-start seasonality and the new category. Best next step is a written SlotBook support agreement, a corrected acknowledgement and matched reporting.

The yield decline is real: gauge R&R is stable, the CMM program and reject criteria are unchanged, and the definition is unchanged. New operators are not worse than experienced ones, and yield fell before they ran alone, so H4 is contradicted. Four changes overlap in time: 12-hour shifts, the Corvane steel, the deferred spindle service and rising hardness spread. L3-02 and L3-05 have worse runout, but they also run the tighter-tolerance long shaft, so R2 is only an association. The scrap-tag timing is a recording artifact, so fatigue is unestablished. The deferral of the service was driven by backlog pressure. The causes cannot be separated without the Line 6 spare lathe CMM data or a staggered service with Tamsworth trial lots (A2). Punishing operators or cutting inspection would be harmful.

The backlog growth is mostly self-generated. First-contact issues rose only 4% (8,770 to 9,120), and Payroll first-contact volume is about 380 a month. Agent-created split tickets rose from 240 to 3,710 a month, customer duplicates from 410 to 2,770, and the 14-day reopen rate from 6% to 23%. Quick-win cherry-picking began three days after the quota and reached 41% of picks. The exempt Billing-Compliance pod stayed flat. Capacity was roughly unchanged (6,020 to 5,960 scheduled hours), and the reopen metric is not a configuration artifact. Resignations are confounded by a rival employer paying 15% more and a deferred pay review. Engineering bugs rose from 40 to 71, so their effect on aged tickets is unestablished. Suspend the per-agent quota, move to team quality measures, and classify the aged tickets. Do not raise the quota or hire yet.

System records show the backlog growth is mostly self-generated. First-contact demand rose only 4% (8,770 to 9,120). Split children rose from 240 to 3,710 and customer duplicates from 410 to 2,770. The reopen rate went from 6% to 23%, and the audit log rules out a reporting artifact. Agents moved from oldest-first picking (71% to 34%) to a quick-wins filter (41% of picks), and aged complex tickets tripled. Capacity was flat (38 to 37 FTE, hours nearly unchanged), and Payroll is a small share of volume. The quota gaming hypothesis is supported, so raising the quota is harmful and extra headcount is premature. Suspend the per-agent quota and classify the aged tickets. Engineering's bug backlog is unquantified.

Reported on-time rose because promised dates were revised, not because delivery improved. Revisions per 100 shipments rose about 5x from March 2026 at each center, and Pell Junction rose only in July. Customer-requested revisions stayed flat at 1.6 vs 1.8 per 100, while Operational-Capacity reasons rose from 22% to 74%. More revisions were entered late, and fewer notified the customer. Brightwell's receiving log shows 81% on or before the booked date, vs 87% a year earlier, against a reported 98.4%. RouteWise and portal explanations fail on timing. Vacancy is only associated with revisions and is confounded by lane length. Suspend the claim and re-base the incentive. Do not launch the campaign or raise the bonus. Hold the driver spend.

The absence rise is mostly a recording artifact. ShiftLine went live on 2026-03-30 and began logging partial-day absences, which the old process did not record. Full-day absences rose only 1.1%. The independent dispatch log shows unchanged unstaffed trips and late pull-outs, so real attendance did not change. Route groups with no recovery cut and no construction held on-time performance at about 82%. Both groups with cut recovery time fell, and the five construction corridor routes fell most (83.5% to 52.5%). The cause is the April recovery cuts plus the construction lane reductions. Higher early-leave rates on cut routes are confounded by seniority and route length. Do not adopt the discipline program. Restore recovery time, set construction running times, and restate the absence data.

Agency spend growth is mostly volume (about 77%), not price (about 23%, tied to a contractual wage-index escalator). Vacancies and resignations have risen steadily since early 2024, before St. Brennan's opened in March 2026. A workload loop is supported: unit-level lagged correlations peak at two quarters, the exit-interview top reason is workload at 49% (pay 17%), and the 4 West pilot cut charge load and exhaustion, with resignations falling against matched units. The 2025 sign-on bonus did not stop vacancy growth, and the CFO plan would suspend the charge and preceptor differentials, which worsens the loop. Extend the 4 West model. Treat rate renegotiation as a secondary lever. Time-to-hire and the falls link remain unestablished.

The yield decline is real: gauge R&R is stable, the CMM program is unchanged, and tolerances are the same (E4, E2). The new-operator hypothesis is contradicted, since new and experienced operators reject at similar rates and yield fell before any of them ran alone (E14). Several causes remain live and the evidence does not separate them. Hardness spread rose in September lots (E7). Spindle runout exceeds the limit on L3-02 and L3-05, and vibration is rising (E10). Every machine worsened, and the long-shaft machines run tighter tolerances (E11). Fatigue is untested because no hour-of-shift data was collected. The best next step is a staggered spindle service with Tamsworth trial lots and hour-of-machining reconstruction. Reverting shifts, cancelling Corvane, penalizing operators and cutting inspection are premature or harmful.

Ticket records contradict deprioritisation of Arts: matched on category and priority, Arts is within 0.3 days of others. The gap comes mainly from SlotBook tickets (42% of Arts tickets) auto-routed to P4 under RR-17, which closes 70% of the gap. The rest comes from Tuesday/Thursday-only on-site cover at Lindqvist, and Education shows the same pattern. Volume is not fully explained by SlotBook, and duplicate rates are normal. The P4 acknowledgement gives no priority or timeframe. Whether Arts leadership was told of RR-17 is undetermined. Best actions are to agree SlotBook's support status, fix the acknowledgement and report split metrics. Blanket P4 is harmful, and a separate desk or decommissioning is premature.

Turnover rise is real, not a PeopleCore artifact: payroll-reconciled counts (115 to 193 separations) and monthly voluntary exits both show it. It exceeds the in-state peer median rise (33% to 38%). Voluntary exits stepped up in March 2026, when the firm-wide two-Saturday policy took effect, before ShiftWise went live on 2026-04-13. Monthly exits were flat afterward. Pay, manager and ShiftWise effects are not yet separated, because there is no branch-level or ShiftWise-versus-non-ShiftWise data and no pay benchmark. The manager-of-record field is stale for the seven branches that changed managers, so tying bonuses to it would punish the wrong people. A 15% raise is premature. Collect the branch-level data and the pay benchmark first. Note: I read 8 evidence files, over the 6-item limit.

The 30% ticket revenue drop is mostly explained by the forced move to Brightwater and wider regional decline, not by programming. Single-ticket sales fell 45% in the relocation year. Lapsed patrons cite travel and parking most often. The cathedral, which is close to the rail station, sold far better. Peer orchestras with no venue change fell about 29%. Concerts with and without post-1945 works sell the same at the same venue. Committed subscribers renew at a stable 85%. Marketing effectiveness cannot be assessed without attribution data. Non-renewal or cutting commissions would put the Halvorsen and Arts Council grants at risk. Present a segmented analysis, separate the artistic review from the revenue question, and use the cathedral dates and a shuttle.

Group ticket time rose about 4 minutes in all nine locations in October 2024, exactly as the board's study projected and accepted, with a 19-minute ceiling. Satisfaction and food quality rose, and speed scores were unchanged, so group-wide inefficiency and satisfaction erosion are not supported. Riverside's spike began after the saute/pasta cook left in August, with the KDS delay concentrated at that station, the vacancy unfilled and transfers deferred by group operations. Other locations show no staffing spread. Delgado's reason for leaving is unresolved, so GM replacement is unjustified. A 2023 audit showed ticket-time bonuses induce KDS gaming. Restore Riverside staffing and reset the benchmark. Do not freeze the menu or add the bonus.

Arts' 9-day median is mostly explained by SlotBook tickets (42% of Arts tickets) sent to the P4 best-effort queue under RR-17, with a 17-day median wait before first action. The remaining gap comes from Tuesday/Thursday-only on-site cover at Lindqvist. Like-for-like Arts and non-Arts remote tickets are within 0.3 days, so deprioritisation of Arts is contradicted. Duplicate rates are similar, so trivial or duplicate filing is contradicted. The P4 acknowledgement gives no priority or timeframe. Whether ITS told Arts leadership of RR-17 is undetermined: a meeting occurred but no record of its content exists. The SSO link to the SlotBook rise is confounded by term start. A written support agreement and a clearer acknowledgement are low-regret. Moving all Arts tickets to P4, or setting up a separate Arts desk, is not supported.

The 98.1% on-time figure appears to be produced by moving promised dates, not by better delivery. Revisions rose 5x. Each center's jump coincides with its bonus start: Northgate and Riverside in March, Pell Junction in July. RouteWise went live in February and Northgate's on-time rate stayed at 91% through Feb, so RouteWise does not explain the jump. Revisions are now mostly capacity-coded, late-entered and rarely customer-notified. Customer-requested revisions per 100 shipments are flat. Brightwell's receiving log shows 81% on time against the booked date, down from 87%, versus the 98.4% scorecard. Dispatchers report pressure to protect the number. The campaign and a higher bonus are harmful. Recomputing against original dates and re-basing the incentive are preferred. The driver-shortage claim is unestablished, and the $2.1M hiring plan is premature.

The rise in ED length of stay for admitted patients is almost entirely boarding (about 3.0 of 3.2 hours). Boarding jumped in March 2026, when the hospitalist rounding change took effect. After it, before-noon medical-ward discharges fell from 29% to 9%. ED RN hours per visit, vacancy and grid compliance were flat. Capacity, occupancy and ED work-up time were also flat. A huddle pilot with a schedule-determined, comparable control cut boarding from 4.6 to 2.3 hours. Extend the huddle. Do not fund travel nurses by deferring case managers, and do not pull the 4 West huddle. Longer door-to-provider time and left-without-being-seen are confounded by the May discontinuation of triage providers. The evening bed-cleaning cut is unmeasured.

Arts is not deprioritised like-for-like: matched-category, matched-priority Arts medians are within 0.3 days of others. SlotBook tickets (42% of Arts tickets) are all routed to P4 and explain 70% of the gap. Most of the remainder comes from Tuesday/Thursday-only technician coverage at Lindqvist, which also affects Education. Non-SlotBook volume is still 1.6x average, so SlotBook does not fully explain volume. Duplicate rates are normal, so trivial or duplicate filing is not the driver. The ACK-P4 template gives requesters no priority or timeframe. Whether ITS told Arts leadership of RR-17 is undocumented. Best next steps are a written SlotBook support agreement, a fixed acknowledgement and matched reporting. ITS's proposal to put all Arts tickets on P4 and the Dean's desk transfer are not justified.

The yield fall is real (stable CMM gauge R&R, program and criteria), so H5 holds. The new-operator cohort is exonerated: their reject rates match experienced operators, and yield was already falling before they ran alone. Three candidate causes remain confounded: deferred spindle service (runout and vibration rising, L3-02 and L3-05 worst), the Corvane bar change (higher hardness spread, but lots ran in sequence with time), and 12-hour fatigue. Scrap tag times are batch-written, so the evidence for fatigue is an artifact. Reverting shifts or cancelling Corvane now would be premature, and sampling inspection or punishing operators would be harmful. The staggered service plus Tamsworth trial and cycle-counter matching is the discriminating next step. The Line 6 Corvane results (X3) are the best single request.
